strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies gap in existing work (visual-centric vs. audio-centric control) and proposes unified multi-modal framework for joint audio-video generation

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple quantitative metrics (Sync-C/D, Text CLIP, Subject DINO), human evaluation with 20 participants across 6 criteria, qualitative comparisons across control modalities
Practical architecture design: MMCU provides elegant unified interface for heterogeneous inputs; Dual-Stream Bypass preserves pretrained weights; zero-initialization ensures training stability
Efficient training: 7,200 steps in 12 hours on 4 H200s demonstrates practical scalability without excessive computational requirements
Flexible inference control: Modality-specific guidance scaling (Figure 7) enables intuitive decoupled control over visual identity and audio timbre, with clear ablation showing effect
Audio quality analysis: Appendix B evaluates speaker similarity, naturalness (UTMOS), and transcription accuracy beyond just synchronization metrics
Clear presentation: Well-structured paper with informative architecture diagrams (Figures 2-3), effective qualitative comparisons, and comprehensive results tables
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: Bypass architecture adapts ControlNet/T2I-Adapter patterns straightforwardly; MMCU is standard concatenation+masking; guidance scaling is simple multiplicative factor. Strong engineering but limited fundamental innovation

Critical missing ablations: No analysis of MMCU design choices; no study of what bypass branches learn or their individual contributions; no ablation of bypass injection points (why even-numbered layers?); limited guidance scaling analysis (single example)

Severe evaluation scope limitation: All evaluation confined to portrait/talking-head animation (single character). Trained on 30K portrait-only Hallo3 data. No evaluation on diverse scenes, full-body motion, multiple characters, or complex backgrounds. Directly contradicts problem framing as 'joint audio-video generation' which implies broader domain

Strong proprietary model dependency: Entire approach builds on unreleased LTX-2. No ablation showing MMControl's contribution vs. base model capability. Reproducibility severely compromised. Cannot assess how much improvement comes from MMCU/bypass vs. LTX-2 inherent quality

Unfair experimental comparison (Table 1): MMControl jointly generates speech+video (harder); baselines use ground-truth audio+first frame (easier). Different tasks conflated. Sync-D higher for baselines (10.2-10.7 vs 10.5), indicating trade-offs not acknowledged

Underdeveloped audio control: Acoustic MMCU minimal (reference audio + silence placeholders). Paper explicitly states pitch/energy contours are 'future extensions.' No comparison with audio-centric methods (MoCha, Wan2.2-S2V) from related work. Acoustic timbre control underanalyzed

Insufficient structural control analysis: Mean MAE 4.52 shows incremental improvement over VACE (5.35). Only qualitative pose comparisons. No systematic analysis of fine-grained pose detail consistency. Quantitative pose error metrics absent

Statistical rigor gaps: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests on quantitative results. Human evaluation modest (20 participants × 5 samples = 100 ratings). No inter-rater agreement (Cohen's κ) reported. Improvements appear small without significance analysis (e.g., 0.2546 vs 0.2337 Text CLIP)

Reproducibility concerns: Depends on proprietary Qwen2.5-Omni for captions; preprocessing uses proprietary tools (Grounded-SAM-2, Depth-Anything-v2, DWPose); no code release mentioned; training details incomplete (warmup schedule, gradient clipping, augmentation specifics)

Limited failure analysis: No discussion of failure modes or edge cases. Single example for decoupled control (Figure 7). Missing analysis: What happens with conflicting conditions (pose vs. text)? How does method handle unseen speech styles or accents?

Incomplete inference analysis: Computational overhead of bypasses vs. baseline unclear. CFG disabled in Stage 2 unjustified. Batch size effects on guidance scaling unexamined. Potential γv-γa interactions unexplored

Ethical considerations absent: Portrait generation with identity+voice control raises deepfake concerns. No discussion of societal impact or misuse prevention despite clear practical applications in synthetic media

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gap in controllable joint audio-video generation where existing methods focus on single modalities
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple well-chosen metrics (Sync-C/D, Text CLIP, Subject DINO, MAE), diverse baselines, and human evaluation across 6 criteria with 20 participants
Strong empirical results: achieves highest Sync-C despite baselines having ground-truth audio advantage; best structural control (depth MAE 4.52, pose MAE 3.07); highest user study score (3.58/4.0)

Thoughtful system design with MMCU elegantly unifying heterogeneous inputs, Dual-Stream Bypass preserving pretrained priors through frozen backbone, and Modality-Specific Guidance Scaling enabling flexible inference-time control
Proper ablation studies (Table S3) demonstrating importance of individual components including MMCU masking and projector weight inheritance
Thorough audio quality evaluation with speaker similarity, UTMOS naturalness, and transcription accuracy metrics
Clear presentation with effective architectural diagrams and diverse qualitative results
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Dual-Stream Bypass resembles ControlNet/T2I-Adapter, MMCU is straightforward concatenation with binary masking (no justification vs. alternatives), and two-stage inference borrowed from LTX-2. Primary contribution is application rather than fundamental innovation.
No comparison with concurrent joint audio-video generation models (Sora 2, Veo 3, MOVA, Universe-1 mentioned but not evaluated), limiting SOTA claims to single-modality baselines only

Narrow evaluation scope: training on only 30,000 proprietary Hallo3 samples; modest test benchmark (200 samples per task); comparison with AVControl limited to depth/pose only; no audio evaluation on same 200 samples as visual

Restricted applicability: evaluated only on single-character portrait animation; acknowledged inability to handle multi-character or conversational settings; no analysis of scalability to longer sequences or complex scenes

Insufficient technical justification for design choices: why is binary masking optimal (no soft-masking or learned routing comparison)? Why omit audio-to-video cross-attention in bypasses (B4 ablation shows degradation but lacks analysis)? Why freeze backbone (no fine-tuning ablation)?
Missing key ablations: effect of Stage 1 resolution (h/2 × w/2) not studied; sensitivity analysis for guidance scaling factors γv, γa not provided

Limited analysis of method behavior: no error cases discussed; no cross-modal interaction analysis (does audio quality affect video?); no visualization of what bypass branches learn; no investigation of conflicting multimodal conditions

Evaluation metric concerns: Text CLIP similarity uniformly low (~0.24) suggesting limited discriminativity; Subject DINO varies widely (0.55–0.89) raising robustness questions; audio evaluation only on 150 samples; WER captures accuracy but not prosody naturalness or emotional expression
Reproducibility concerns: training on proprietary Hallo3 dataset; no code/model release mentioned; some architectural details unspecified; no inference-time cost analysis
Societal impact discussion absent despite application to synthetic talking-head generation with misuse potential; no mention of watermarking or detection methods
